problem: RL-trained exploration policies such as Active Neural SLAM (ANS) overfit to the statistics of their training environments. When trained on Gibson (offices) and deployed in out-of-distribution environments such as MP3D (larger, irregular homes), they explore noticeably less area. ANS's global-policy actor-critic uses plain CNN + FC layers, which do not have the geometric symmetries the task implies.
motivation: Exploration is a geometric problem. The actor maps a 2D map state to a 2D long-term-goal map, so it should be translation- and rotation-equivariant. The critic outputs expected future coverage, so it should be rotation-invariant but not translation- or scale-invariant. Building these inductive biases into the architecture shrinks the hypothesis space and should reduce overfitting, which data augmentation cannot guarantee for OOD test data.
key_idea: Redesign ANS's global policy so the actor becomes (approximately) rotation- and translation-equivariant and the critic becomes rotation-invariant but not translation-invariant. This uses p4 G-convolutions, blur pooling, and a new semi-global polar pooling (SGPP) layer.
insight: Matching the architecture's symmetries exactly to the task matters, and excess invariance hurts. In the ablation (figures only) the ranking is S-ANS > E-ANS (no SGPP, critic lacks rotation invariance) > G-ANS (SGPP replaced by global average pooling, which adds unwanted translation invariance to the critic) > ANS. So superfluous translation invariance hurts more than missing rotation invariance. The gains come mostly under domain shift (+8.1 m² on MP3D vs +0.8 m² on Gibson). Analysis confirms the critic actually becomes more rotation-invariant: output std over 24 rotations drops 0.115→0.078 (Gibson) and 0.160→0.084 (MP3D), and feature cosine similarity across rotations rises 0.06→0.40 and 0.07→0.55. The FBE-RL baseline beats heuristic FBE on Gibson but loses on MP3D, illustrating that learned policies overfit.
method: ANS base framework: neural SLAM builds a 4-channel global map (obstacles, explored, agent position, visited path). The global policy (A2C actor-critic) takes a rescaled global view plus a cropped local view and outputs a long-term goal. A planner produces short-term goals, and a local policy outputs actions.

Symmetry analysis: derives the ideal properties (actor translation- and rotation-equivariant, not scale-equivariant; critic rotation-invariant, not translation- or scale-invariant, with rotation equivariance required up to the last conv layer). It then identifies that ANS's CNN lacks rotation equivariance/invariance.

p4 G-convolution: replaces all standard convs in the shared conv block with p4 group convolutions (filters rotated by mπ/2, m=0..3), giving approximate rotation equivariance. The FC layers of the actor are kept and left to learn equivariance.
Blur pooling: replaces max pooling (anti-aliased downsampling) so the conv block stays accurately translation-equivariant.

Semi-global polar pooling (SGPP): placed in the critic between the shared conv block and the FC layers. It converts the feature map from Cartesian to polar coordinates (ρ, φ) and average-pools over φ, giving a c×h descriptor. This is rotation-invariant but not translation- or scale-invariant.

setting.backbone: ANS (neural SLAM + local policy) with redesigned global-policy actor-critic: p4 G-CNN + blur pooling + SGPP + FC layers, trained from scratch with RL (A2C)
setting.training_data: RL in Habitat on Gibson training scenes (main); additional experiment trained on MP3D. No extra data.
setting.observation: egocentric depth + noisy pose/odometry (noisy actuation and sensing at train and test)
setting.action_space: global policy predicts long-term goal on a 2D map; planner + local policy output low-level discrete actions

numbers_note: The metric is area coverage in m² (not SR/SPL). The paper calls the evaluation sets the 'test splits' of Gibson and MP3D. It follows the ANS/OccupancyAnticipation protocol, where the Gibson evaluation scenes are the Gibson val set, so the split labels may not match other papers. The ablation variants (E-ANS, G-ANS) and the MP3D-trained S-ANS tested on Gibson are shown only as curves in figures, with no printed numbers. Rotation-invariance diagnostics (critic output std, feature cosine similarity) are analysis-only and not included as benchmark numbers.
results: Trained on Gibson, S-ANS improves area coverage over the strongest baseline, ANS, from 32.9 to 33.7 m² on Gibson (in-distribution) and from 76.3 to 84.4 m² on MP3D (OOD, +8.1 m²). It also beats FBE (26.5 / 69.6) and FBE-RL (28.2 / 63.0). When trained and tested on MP3D, S-ANS reaches 86.2 vs 80.8 m² for ANS. The gap between S-ANS trained on Gibson and trained on MP3D (84.4 vs 86.2) is smaller than the corresponding gap for ANS (76.3 vs 80.8).
limitations: Only discrete 90° (p4) rotation equivariance is built in, and the actor's FC layers are not equivariant, so the symmetries are only approximate.

Evaluated only on visual exploration (area coverage) within the ANS framework on Gibson/MP3D with a small baseline set. The in-distribution gain is small (+0.8 m²), and ablation results appear only in figures.
Assumes the map state is the relevant input. Symmetry benefits for goal-directed navigation tasks or real robots are not tested.
